analysis.one_liner: Extends children's online privacy protections to teens and bans targeted advertising to minors.
analysis.headline: The House Energy and Commerce Committee approved the bill by voice vote in September 2024, but it was never brought to the House floor and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill updates the 1998 children's online privacy law to cover teenagers ages 13 to 16, not just children under 13. It would stop websites and apps from using kids' personal data to target them with ads, let parents and teens view and delete collected data, require stronger security, and let the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general enforce the rules. The committee approved it unanimously by voice vote, but House leadership never scheduled a vote on the floor before the two-year Congress expired.
analysis.who_benefits: Children under 13 and teens 13 through 16 who use websites, apps, games, and connected devices, plus their parents, who gain the right to review, correct, and delete the data companies collect about their kids.

how_it_helps.text: The bill extends the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act from children under 13 to cover 'teens,' defined as individuals over 12 and under 17, so platforms are restricted in how they collect and use teen data [S2].

It makes it unlawful for operators with actual knowledge, or knowledge fairly implied by objective circumstances, that a user is a child or teen to collect, use, disclose, or maintain their personal information for individual-specific advertising, except for contextual ads and ads the user asks for [S2].

It requires operators to give parents and teens notice of data practices, verifiable consent for collection, access to the data collected, the ability to delete data and refuse further use, the ability to challenge inaccuracies, and reasonable security protections [S2].

The bill expands the definition of personal information to cover persistent identifiers like IP addresses and device IDs, geolocation, biometric data such as facial templates and voiceprints, and photos or audio of a child's image or voice [S2].

The FTC and state attorneys general are given explicit authority to enforce the new prohibitions, and the FTC must report annually to Congress on its enforcement actions, investigations, and complaints under the law [S2].

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the cost would fall on social media platforms, app developers, and digital ad companies, whose ad businesses run on collecting and profiling user data, including data about young users, and who would face FTC enforcement and state lawsuits for violations.

drawbacks.text: The bill explicitly does not require operators to verify ages or implement age gating, relying instead on operators' 'knowledge fairly implied on the basis of objective circumstances,' so companies could avoid the law's protections if they can plausibly claim they did not know a user's age [S2].

Its protections for teens depend on teens themselves giving consent to collection, and it permits operators to terminate service to a child or teen whose parent or the teen refuses further data collection, so the leverage in the notice-and-consent system still sits with the company [S2].

It creates a written-agreement pathway for education technology operators to collect student data without verifiable consent, shifting enforcement of children's privacy in schools from families to school systems [S2].
It exempts nonprofits that would be exempt from the FTC Act, leaving data practices of nonprofit online services unregulated by this law [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The privacy gains for children and teens are real and address a widely felt problem: platforms currently profile and target kids with personalized ads. The main weakness is that without any age-verification duty, the law depends on catching companies that should have known a user was a minor, which creates a loophole companies can design around. Even a strong honest supporter would concede the compliance costs fall hardest on small app developers, though the bill requires the FTC to analyze small-business impacts. On balance, the benefits to families outweigh the costs to industry.

outcome.mechanism: The House committee held a markup and approved it by voice vote in September 2024, but it was never reported to and voted on by the full House before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Tim Walberg (R-MI) introduced the bill on April 9, 2024, with bipartisan original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1][S2].
Twenty-eight members cosponsored the bill, split 16 Democrats and 12 Republicans [S3].
On September 18, 2024, the Energy and Commerce Committee held a markup session and ordered the bill reported to the House, as amended, by voice vote [S4].
No further action appears in the record: the bill was never reported out of committee to the floor, never debated, and never voted on before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Platforms and the adtech industry, which continue profiling and targeting children and teens under the pre-2024 rules; families gained nothing from this Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan: a Republican sponsor with 16 Democratic and 12 Republican cosponsors, and a committee that approved it by voice vote with no recorded opposition.

industries.note: The bill restricts how platforms collect and use personal data from users under 17, including requiring consent and data deletion rights. Platforms' revenue model relies on exactly this data collection, and the outcome preserved the status quo for them.

The bill bans individual-specific advertising to children and teens based on profiling or persistent identifiers, cutting off targeted ad revenue from young users. The bill never became law, so this revenue stream was untouched.

The bill would let edtech operators collect student data without verifiable parental consent if they sign written agreements with schools limiting use to educational purposes. That keeps schools as a channel for data collection while adding notice and review requirements.
